# Strux OS Documentation

> Build a bootable kiosk Linux image from a web frontend and a Go backend, develop on real hardware, write board support packages, and ship signed updates.

## Guide

- [Backend](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/backend.html): Your backend is a plain Go program using the Strux runtime library. It handles everything a browser can't — hardware, files, networking, system control —…
- [Building](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/building.html): strux build turns your project into a complete, bootable OS image. This page is the day-to-day guide: what a build actually does, how to read its output,…
- [Customizing the OS](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/customizing-the-os.html): Your project's strux.yaml controls more than the app — it shapes the operating system itself.
- [Dev Mode](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/dev-mode.html): strux dev is the live development loop: it builds a development image, boots it (in QEMU or connects to a real device using --remote), and keeps your…
- [Flashing](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/flashing.html): Flashing is the step where your built image leaves your laptop and lands on real hardware — written to a board's eMMC (built-in flash storage), an SD card,…
- [Frontend](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/frontend.html): Your frontend is a normal web app — this page covers the one Strux-specific part: how it talks to your Go backend through an automatically generated, fully…
- [Getting Started](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/getting-started.html): This page takes you from nothing to a Strux OS image booting in a virtual machine.
- [Installation](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/installation.html): This page gets the strux CLI installed on your machine, along with the tools it needs. Five minutes, then you're ready for Getting Started.
- [Introduction](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/introduction.html): Strux OS is a framework for building kiosk-style Linux operating systems.
- [Project Structure](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/project-structure.html): This page walks through every file and folder in a Strux project — what it's for, what you should edit, and what Strux manages for you.
- [Running in QEMU](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/running-qemu.html): strux run boots your built image in QEMU — a virtual machine that emulates your target hardware — so you can see exactly what a device will do, from splash…
- [Updates](https://docs.strux.sh/guide/updates.html): A kiosk in the field needs a way to receive new software without someone driving out with an SD card.

## Concepts

- [Artifacts](https://docs.strux.sh/concepts/artifacts.html): Strux embeds a lot of source inside the CLI binary itself: the on-device startup scripts, systemd services, the Cage compositor's C source, the Strux…
- [Board Support Packages](https://docs.strux.sh/concepts/bsp.html): A Board Support Package (BSP) is a folder in your project that teaches Strux how to build for one specific piece of hardware.
- [Build Pipeline](https://docs.strux.sh/concepts/build-pipeline.html): When you run strux build, the CLI executes a fixed sequence of steps, each one a shell script running inside the strux-builder Docker container.
- [Caching](https://docs.strux.sh/concepts/caching.html): A full Strux build compiles a browser stack and assembles a Debian system — that can take a long time.
- [Display Stack](https://docs.strux.sh/concepts/display-stack.html): This page explains how your web app gets onto physical screens: the Cage compositor, the Cog browser, and the display configuration in strux.yaml that maps…
- [Architecture Overview](https://docs.strux.sh/concepts/overview.html): This page explains how Strux works under the hood, in two halves: what happens on your machine when you run strux build, and what happens on the device…
- [Update System](https://docs.strux.sh/concepts/update-system.html): This page explains how Strux OTA updates work internally: the .struxb bundle format, the signing and verification model, and how a device installs an update…

## Board support packages

- [Dual Rootfs & A/B Updates](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/concepts/dual-rootfs.html): This page explains how Strux applies a full-system update on a device without risking a brick: two root filesystem slots, A and B.
- [The Runtime Extension System](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/concepts/extension-system.html): A BSP can ship Go code that runs inside your application on the device.
- [Lifecycle Scripts](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/concepts/lifecycle-scripts.html): A BSP customizes the build by attaching shell scripts to hooks in the build pipeline — points before and after each built-in step.
- [Bootloaders](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/guide/bootloader.html): This page covers the boot.bootloader block of bsp.yaml: bootloader types, the built-in U-Boot build, bootloader-level device trees, boot methods, and the…
- [BSP Examples](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/guide/examples.html): The fastest way to write a BSP is to start from one that already works.
- [Flash Scripts](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/guide/flash-scripts.html): strux flash gets a built image onto real hardware — over USB, onto an SD card, however your board is programmed.
- [BSP Development](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/guide/introduction.html): This track is for developers bringing Strux up on new hardware — taking a board that ships with a vendor Linux image (or nothing at all) and turning it into…
- [Custom Kernels](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/guide/kernel.html): This page covers the boot.kernel block of bsp.yaml: choosing a kernel source, configuring it with a defconfig and fragments, applying patches, building…
- [Runtime Extensions](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/guide/runtime-extensions.html): A runtime extension is a Go package inside your BSP that gives the Strux runtime board-specific hardware control — backlight, network management, Wi-Fi, or…
- [Writing Lifecycle Scripts](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/guide/scripts.html): Lifecycle scripts are how your BSP does board-specific work the generic build pipeline can't: assembling the final disk image, patching kernel sources,…
- [Writing a BSP](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/guide/writing-a-bsp.html): This guide walks you from an empty folder to a BSP that builds a flashable image for real hardware.
- [bsp.yaml Reference](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/reference/bsp-yaml.html): Every key that bsp.yaml accepts, with types, defaults, and accepted values.
- [Build Steps & Lifecycle Hooks](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/reference/build-steps.html): The exact order of the build pipeline, what each step does, when conditional steps run, and the full list of before_* / after_* hook values your BSP scripts…
- [Environment Variables](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/reference/environment-variables.html): Every environment variable Strux sets for BSP scripts, plus the variables the strux CLI itself reads from your shell.
- [Path Resolution](https://docs.strux.sh/bsp/reference/path-resolution.html): How Strux resolves the paths you write in a script entry's cached_generated_artifacts and depends_on in bsp.yaml.

## Reference

- [CLI Reference](https://docs.strux.sh/reference/cli.html): Every strux command, argument, and flag. For task-oriented walkthroughs, see the Getting Started guide — this page is the lookup table.
- [Frontend API Reference](https://docs.strux.sh/reference/frontend-api.html): Everything your web frontend can call on the Go backend: your app's own fields and methods, the built-in window.strux.* system services, and the…
- [Go Runtime Reference](https://docs.strux.sh/reference/go-runtime.html): Every exported function, method, and type in the Strux Go runtime library (github.com/strux-dev/strux/pkg/runtime).
- [strux.yaml Reference](https://docs.strux.sh/reference/strux-yaml.html): Every key in strux.yaml, the project configuration file at the root of a Strux project.
